There is no wild lemon: it is a cross between two other fruits, the citron and the bitter orange. Its juice runs 5–6% citric acid, which is what the sourness is. It reached Europe near southern Italy by the second century AD.

The plant barely bothers with seed: it throws out runners, pegs them down until they root, and the new plant is cut free. That is how strawberries were propagated in Europe for centuries before anyone bred them.
The banana plant is the largest herbaceous flowering plant there is — no wood, no trunk, just a pseudostem of rolled-up leaf stalks. The fruit is a berry, and cultivated ones carry no fertile seed.
Summer and autumn pears are climacteric — harvested before they are ripe, still green, and they snap off cleanly when lifted. The ripening happens after the harvest.
Like most temperate-latitude trees, a cherry needs a certain number of chilling hours each year to break dormancy and bloom at all. A mild winter is not a kindness to a cherry tree.
A fig is a syconium: a hollow fleshy structure lined on the inside with flowers. A single narrow opening at the tip lets the fig wasp Blastophaga psenes crawl in to pollinate them.

Coffee beans are not beans. They are the seeds of a fruit — the coffee cherry — separated out of the flesh to give green, unroasted beans. The earliest reports of anyone drinking it are among the Sufis of Yemen in the mid-15th century.
Roasting is what makes coffee taste of coffee: heat breaks the bean's starches into simple sugars that caramelise and brown. Then grind it, steep it in hot water, and filter the grounds back out.
Unlike most fruiting trees, the cacao pod grows directly from the trunk or a large branch rather than from twigs. Inside are the seeds — 30 to 40 beans to a typical pod.

The pods and their pulp are heaped up for several days and left to sweat: the thick pulp liquefies as it ferments. Sweating is what the quality depends on — without it the beans keep a strong, bitter taste.

Roasted, cracked and deshelled into nibs, then ground to a paste. Conching takes the particles under about 20 μm — smaller than the tongue can detect — which is what "smooth" actually means. Four hundred beans to the pound.
Collagen is a quarter to a third of all the protein in a mammal, and about 35% of collagen is glycine — one at almost every third residue. Nothing else in a body is that concentrated a source.

The glucose-alanine cycle. Muscle burning amino acids for fuel collects the loose amino groups onto glutamate, hands one to pyruvate to make alanine, and puts that into the blood for the liver to sort out.
Serine hydroxymethyltransferase runs both ways. Normally it cleaves serine into glycine and a spare carbon handed to folate — but with glycine in excess it runs backwards and builds serine instead.
Proline is made from glutamate, and it is the only one of the twenty whose nitrogen is a secondary amine — the side chain closes back onto it. Plants pile proline up as a standard response to stress.
Phenylalanine hydroxylase is a monooxygenase: it hangs a hydroxyl on the end of phenylalanine's ring and the result is tyrosine. Lacking that one enzyme is what phenylketonuria is.
Transamination: aspartate transaminase moves an amino group between glutamate and aspartate, and oxaloacetate is what receives it. That same enzyme is the AST on a liver blood test.

Glutamate is the hub. Transamination of alpha-ketoglutarate makes it, and it then hands its own amino group on to build the others — tissues collect loose nitrogen as glutamate before doing anything else with it.
Glutamine synthetase sticks ammonia straight onto glutamate. Free ammonia is toxic and glutamine is not, so this is how nitrogen travels in the blood without doing damage on the way.

Asparagine synthetase builds it from aspartate, glutamine and ATP: aspartate is the skeleton, glutamine donates the nitrogen for the amide. Heat this with a reducing sugar later and you get acrylamide.

Glutamate becomes ornithine; ornithine takes on a carbamoyl group built from ammonia and bicarbonate; two steps later, arginine. Arginase then splits it into urea and ornithine and the cycle starts again.
Valine is built from pyruvic acid — sugar, three carbons in — by a run of enzymes that bacteria and plants have and animals do not. That absence is the whole of what essential means.

Leucine and valine come off the same line: plants and microbes build leucine from pyruvic acid, and valine synthesis uses the initial part of that same pathway. Animals run neither, so both are essential.
In plants isoleucine is assembled from two other amino acids — threonine and methionine. Both of those are essential to you as well, so it is essentials all the way down.

Plants and bacteria build it from aspartic acid by way of homoserine, which gets a phosphate hung on it and then knocked off again with the hydroxyl shifted. Animals run none of that, so you have to eat it.
The backbone comes from aspartic acid and the sulfur comes from cysteine, along the transsulfuration pathway. Run the trade the other way and methionine's sulfur is what ends up in cysteine.

Lysine is the limiting amino acid in most cereal grains — the essential one present in the smallest quantity — and it is plentiful in pulses. That is the entire nutritional case for eating the two together.
Histidine is the odd one out: the first reaction of its pathway condenses ATP with PRPP, so the molecule the cell spends as currency is also the one it takes apart to build this amino acid's ring.

Bacteria, fungi, algae and plants build phenylalanine through the shikimate pathway and animals cannot. Industry gets round that by fermenting sugar with E. coli, in bulk, for food uses including aspartame.
The last step is tryptophan synthase welding an indole ring onto serine. So the largest of the twenty is one of the smaller ones with a ring bolted on the side.
The commonest motifs in collagen are glycine-proline-X and glycine-X-hydroxyproline. Glycine sits at almost every third residue and proline fills much of the rest.
Silk fibroin is the sequence Gly-Ser-Gly-Ala-Gly-Ala repeated over and over, stacked as antiparallel beta sheets. The high glycine content is what lets the sheets pack that tightly.
In mammals cysteine is assembled out of two other amino acids: methionine supplies the sulfur by way of homocysteine, serine supplies the rest, and cystathionine beta-synthase joins them.
Condensation is the change from gas to liquid, and it is exactly the reverse of vaporisation. Cool a vapour to its saturation limit and it has nowhere to go but back to water.

At the melting point the ordering of the molecules in the solid breaks down to a less ordered state, and the solid melts. The temperature stays put while it happens — all the energy goes into the change itself.
Earthenware is fired around 600°C — hot enough to turn clay to ceramic for good, and no hotter. Stop here and you have a pot.
Limestone calcination runs at 900 to 1,050°C: CaCO3 becomes CaO and the carbon dioxide leaves as gas. What is left is quicklime, and it weighs a great deal less.
Slaking. Quicklime and water react hard enough to boil the water, and the calcium hydroxide left behind sets slowly in air back into limestone — which is what lime mortar is.

Fluorite is calcium fluoride, and it forms vein deposits in limestone alongside galena and sphalerite — the lead and zinc ores. The name is from fluere, to flow: it was valued as a flux in iron smelting, to thin the slag.

Kelp is the sea's answer to a plant and is not a plant at all — a brown alga that grips rock with a holdfast instead of rooting, wants shallow water between 6 and 14°C, and can add half a metre in a day.

Borate minerals are water-soluble, so they end up wherever a seasonal lake fills and dries and fills again. Borax was first found in dry lake beds in Tibet, and traded down the Silk Road by the 8th century AD.

The chloralkali process: run a current through concentrated brine and it splits into three useful things at once — chlorine at one electrode, hydrogen at the other, sodium hydroxide left in the cell. 2NaCl + 2H2O → Cl2 + H2 + 2NaOH.

Fluorite is the main source of fluoride and so of fluorine, but getting the element out takes low-temperature electrolysis and nobody managed it until Henri Moissan in 1886. He got the Nobel for it in 1906, two months before he died.

Bromide sits in seawater at 65 parts per million and in the Dead Sea at 0.4%. Bubble chlorine through the brine and the chlorine takes the electrons — Br− is oxidised to Br2 — and a blast of steam or air carries the bromine off.

Kelp was the only commercial source of iodine for a century. Courtois was burning seaweed for saltpetre in 1811, added too much sulfuric acid to the ash, and a cloud of violet vapour came off and settled out as dark crystals.

Sand is silicon dioxide. Reduce it carbothermically with coke in an arc furnace — SiO2 + 2 C → Si + 2 CO — and the carbon walks off with the oxygen. Berzelius got there first in 1824, by a different route entirely.

Boron never appears free on Earth. Gay-Lussac and Thénard reduced boric acid with iron at high temperature to get at it — and even that was not really pure boron, which arguably had to wait for Ezekiel Weintraub in 1909.
Arsenopyrite, FeAsS, is the illustrative arsenic mineral — iron, arsenic and sulfur together. Roast it without air and grey arsenic is what you get.

Copper is refined by electrolysis, and whatever will not dissolve drops to the bottom of the cell as anode mud. Nearly all the world's selenium is picked out of that mud. Berzelius found it in 1817, in the sludge of a sulfuric acid plant.
Roast stibnite to the oxide, then take the oxygen off with carbon: 2 Sb2O3 + 3 C makes 4 Sb and 3 CO2. Lower-grade ore goes through a blast furnace, higher-grade through a reverberatory one.

Mendeleev left a gap below silicon in 1869 and predicted ekasilicon. In 1886 Clemens Winkler pulled a new element out of argyrodite — a silver ore, Ag8GeS6 — and it fitted the prediction. Germanium made the first transistor in 1948.

Tellurium is one of very few elements that bonds to gold in nature — calaverite and sylvanite are gold tellurides. Müller von Reichenstein found it in Transylvanian gold ore in 1782; Klaproth isolated and named it in 1798, for tellus, earth.

Argon-40 is what a potassium-40 atom becomes, and potassium-40 has a half-life of 1.25 billion years. Nearly all the argon in the atmosphere got there that way: decayed out of the crust and let go. It is 0.934% of the air.
Krypton and xenon are both taken out of liquid oxygen, and they come off together — what the plant hands you is a mixture, not either gas on its own.

Manganese only settles out as pyrolusite where conditions are oxidising — in hydrothermal veins, and in bogs, where it grows out of the alteration of other manganese minerals. It is the most important manganese ore there is.

Molybdenite is a sulfide, and it crystallises out of high-temperature hydrothermal ore deposits — most of the world's supply rides along in porphyry copper bodies rather than in molybdenum mines of its own.

Osmiridium turns up in the same platinum-bearing river sands as the platinum itself, in the Urals and in the Americas. It is also how you tell it apart: aqua regia dissolves gold and platinum, and leaves osmiridium sitting there.

Iron-free manganese metal is not smelted at all. The ore is leached with sulfuric acid and the metal pulled out of that solution by electricity — electrowinning. Smelt it in a blast furnace instead and you get ferromanganese: iron with manganese in it.

Cobalt is almost never the thing being mined. It comes up as a by-product of copper and nickel, which is why its supply rides on whether those two are worth digging — and why the Congolese Copperbelt supplies most of the world's cobalt.

You cannot melt tungsten out of anything — nothing else is that hot. Instead the oxide is heated in hydrogen, which takes the oxygen away as steam and leaves grey tungsten powder: WO3 + 3 H2 → W + 3 H2O.

Molybdenite is roasted at 700°C to burn the sulfur off as sulfur dioxide, and the trioxide left behind is then reduced in hydrogen: MoO3 + 3 H2 → Mo + 3 H2O. Two steps, because the sulfur has to go first.

Vanadium mostly is not mined — it is swept up afterwards. Its main source is a vanadium-bearing iron ore, and when that ore is smelted for iron most of the vanadium ends up in the slag, where it is recovered. Ninety per cent of world supply arrives this way.

Cadmium sits as a minor component in nearly every zinc ore, and it is never mined for its own sake. Heat the smelted zinc under vacuum and the cadmium — the lower-boiling of the two — distils off first.
Palladium is not mined on its own. It comes out of nickel–copper deposits alongside platinum, and one Russian nickel company, Norilsk Nickel, accounts for 39% of world production by itself.

Wollaston pulled rhodium out of crude platinum in 1803 and got a rose-coloured sodium salt, sodium hexachlororhodate, which is what the element is named for. Its job now is the third way in a three-way catalytic converter: stripping NOx from exhaust.

Iridium comes out of its natural alloy with osmium, and the last step is a reduction: the iridium chloride salt is heated in hydrogen and what is left is metal powder. It is the most corrosion-resistant metal known, and one of the nine rarest in the crust.

Heat osmium hard enough in air and it stops being solid: it becomes osmium tetroxide, which sublimes at room temperature. Distil that vapour off, reduce it back, and you have the metal. That compound is also the name — osmē is Greek for smell.

Ruthenium's one natural mineral is laurite, a sulfide, and it turns up wherever the other platinum metals do — the Urals, the Americas, and the nickel ore at Sudbury. Commercially it is a by-product of processing nickel, copper and platinum ore.

Rhenium substitutes for molybdenum inside molybdenite, sometimes at a couple of per cent. Roast the ore and the rhenium oxides go up the chimney — which is where it is collected, leached back out of the flue dust. About 80% of supply comes this way.

All hafnium is a by-product of cleaning zirconium up: fuel cladding needs zirconium with the hafnium out, because hafnium's neutron-capture cross-section is 600 times zirconium's. What comes off is then reduced with magnesium, as the zirconium was.

Zirconium comes from zircon, a silicate that survives weathering so well it accumulates in beach sand. The metal is made the same way titanium is — the Kroll process, reducing the chloride with molten magnesium: ZrCl4 + 2 Mg → Zr + 2 MgCl2.

Tantalum metal is made by reducing potassium heptafluorotantalate with sodium in a molten salt bath at around 800°C: K2[TaF7] + 5 Na → Ta + 5 NaF + 2 KF. Its ore, coltan, is also the reason tantalum keeps turning up in accounts of the war in the Congo.

Telling niobium from tantalum took until the 1860s, and the trick is water: their two complex fluoride salts dissolve in it to different degrees, so repeated crystallisation slowly pulls them apart. That is still the basis of the separation.

Nobody mines scandium. In 2003 the whole world supply came out of three mines digging for other things — uranium and iron in Ukraine, rare earths in China, apatite in Russia. The oxide recovered becomes scandium fluoride, reduced with calcium metal.

Yttrium is never free in nature — it rides along in rare-earth minerals and some uranium ores, and has to be picked out of the mixture by ion exchange. Only a few tonnes of metal are made a year, by reducing yttrium fluoride with a calcium–magnesium alloy.

Pollucite is a pegmatite mineral, and pegmatites are where lithium lives too — it turns up in the same rock as spodumene, petalite and lepidolite. Find the lithium pegmatite and you have found the caesium.

Monazite is dense and refuses to weather away, so rivers and surf sort it out of everything lighter and pile it up as heavy mineral sand — the same density trick that concentrates gold in a pan, on a beach-sized scale.

Monazite has to be cracked open before it gives anything up. Hot sodium hydroxide at about 140°C does it — the same lye you get from wood ash, concentrated — dissolving the phosphate away and leaving the rare earths behind as hydroxides.

Baryte is a sulfate, and the classic place to find it is a mineral vein cutting through limestone — the same lead-and-zinc veins miners were already working, with the heavy spar sitting alongside as the stuff nobody wanted.

Most lithium is not mined at all. Brine is pumped up from under a salt flat into shallow ponds and the sun is left to take the water away — the Salar de Atacama alone was producing about a third of the world's supply by 2015.

Caesium was the first element ever found with a spectroscope, in 1860. Getting the metal out is cruder than that sounds: turn the ore into caesium chloride, heat it to 700–800°C with calcium, and distil the caesium off.

Nobody mines rubidium. It comes out as a by-product wherever caesium is being made from pollucite, and the two are so alike that parting them means crystallising the same alum out of solution about thirty times over.
Most beryllium is made by reducing beryllium fluoride with magnesium. Heat the fluoride to 900°C with magnesium and finely divided beryllium forms; take it to 1,300°C and it comes together as metal.

Humphry Davy got the first strontium in 1808 by electrolysing strontium chloride mixed with mercuric oxide — the metal came out as an amalgam with mercury, which then had to be driven off to leave strontium behind.

Barium won't come out by electrolysis — it dissolves back into the molten salt and the product is filthy. So it is made the way chromium is: burn aluminium for the oxygen at 1,100°C and take what's left.

Radium behaves so much like barium that barium is what you use to catch it — then crystallise the two apart over and over, watching the spectroscope for radium's red lines against barium's green. A tonne of ore yields about a seventh of a gram.

Berzelius announced thorium in 1829 and could only get an impure sample, by attacking a thorium fluoride salt with potassium metal. Its ore is monazite sand, which averages about 2.5% thorium — the reason those sands are mildly radioactive.

This is the only element here that is not dug up. U-235 fissions and throws out neutrons; the U-238 sitting next to it catches one, and becomes neptunium, and then plutonium. The two kinds of uranium do it to each other.

There is about 0.1 mg of polonium in a tonne of uranium ore, so nobody extracts it — they make it. Put bismuth in a reactor's neutron flux and bismuth-209 becomes bismuth-210, which beta-decays into polonium.

Roast the mixture and every lanthanide but one turns into the same kind of oxide. Cerium is the exception — it goes all the way to +4, forms CeO2, and that oxide won't dissolve when the others do. Cerium separates itself.

Turn the mixture into lanthanum chloride and then take the chlorine off it with lithium metal: LaCl3 + 3Li → La + 3LiCl. Lanthanum is about a quarter of all the lanthanide content in monazite, so there is plenty of it to take.

Neodymium spent 44 years inside an element that didn't exist: 'didymium', the twin, which Auer von Welsbach finally split in two in 1885. The metal itself comes out of molten halide salts by electrolysis.

Reduce samarium oxide with lanthanum metal, then simply distil the two apart — samarium boils at 1,794°C and lanthanum not until 3,464°C, so the samarium leaves first and the lanthanum stays in the pot.

Europium is the one lanthanide with a back door. Reduce it with zinc and Eu(III) drops to Eu(II), which stops behaving like a rare earth and starts behaving like an alkaline earth — so it can be dropped out with barium sulfate while the rest stay put.

Straightforward, for once: heat gadolinium oxide or one of its salts with calcium metal to 1,450°C under argon, and the calcium takes the oxygen. It is named after Johan Gadolin, by way of the mineral gadolinite.

Promethium isn't in any ore worth digging. It was found in 1945 at Oak Ridge, in the wreckage of fissioned uranium fuel, by ion-exchange chromatography — the technique that finally made the rare earths separable at all. Named for the Titan who stole fire.
Krypton is the more volatile of the two, so warming the mixture drives it off first. The krypton/xenon mixture is separated into krypton and xenon by further distillation.
Xenon is the heavier and less volatile half, and the rarer one — 87 parts per billion of the atmosphere, about one part in 11.5 million. Cool the mixture and it is what stays behind.
Bismuth is not really mined, it is what is left over. Lead refining scrapes it out on purpose — calcium and magnesium go into molten lead at around 380°C and the bismuth leaves with the dross.

Bone is about 30% flexible matrix and 70% bound mineral. The collagen gives it tensile strength and its elasticity resists fracture; the calcium phosphate gives it compressive strength. Neither alone would do — the effects are synergistic.
The chicken eggshell is 95 to 97% calcium carbonate crystals held in a protein matrix — the same mineral, calcite, that shells and limestone are built from.

Molluscs carry an outer layer of tissue called the mantle, and its specialised cells build the shell from minerals and proteins taken from the water around them. Calcium carbonate is the main compound of the structure.

Most grains in limestone are skeletal fragments of marine organisms, left behind when the animals died. Buried under everything that settled after them, pressure dissolves the points where grains touch and redeposits the mineral in the gaps; past about a kilometre down, cementation finishes the job.

Limestone need not be built by anything alive. Calcite precipitates straight out of water holding dissolved calcium, and a rise in temperature or a drop in pressure — either of which drives off dissolved CO2 — is what tips it out of solution.
Waves throw loose rock against itself, and the pieces grind and chip each other progressively smaller, smoother and rounder.
Threshing breaks the ear apart but leaves grain and chaff mixed together. Air sorts them by weight — the light chaff blows aside and the heavy grain falls straight back down.

Fuel cannot burn faster than air reaches it. Force a draught through charcoal and the rate of combustion climbs with the air supply, which is why a smith's hearth has a pipe into the fire and something pumping at the other end.
No salt and no smoke, only cold moving air. About 80% of the water leaves the fish while it hangs on the racks from February to May, and what is left keeps for years.

Hot glass is stiff enough to hold a shape and soft enough to stretch, so a puff of air down a hollow pipe opens a bubble inside a lump of it. Phoenician and Syrian craftsmen had the technique in the first century BC.
A blown-out candle leaves the wick smouldering, and that smouldering wick is where the trail of smoke comes from. A snuffer puts the flame out by depriving it of oxygen instead, and leaves no trail.

About one plant in eight skips insects and posts its pollen into the air instead. Those flowers are small, scentless and offer no nectar, because there is nobody to advertise to — the grains go out by the myriad and a small percentage land where they are needed.

A flame burns in the gas above the fuel, and it needs a steady oxygen supply to stay there. Cut that off and what survives is combustion on the fuel's own surface — slow, flameless, and giving off carbon monoxide at a higher yield than a flaming fire does.

Bone heated in a sealed vessel chars instead of burning. The oxygen has to be kept low, because what suffers first is the adsorption capacity — and that porosity is the whole reason the stuff is worth making.
Shut a kiln's vents and the flames, short of oxygen, start taking it from the iron oxide in the pottery itself. The fabric of the clay changes colour from its natural red to black.
Dry air is 78.08% nitrogen and 20.95% oxygen, with argon at 0.93% and carbon dioxide at 0.04% making up almost all of the last one per cent.

There was no free oxygen in the air until about 2.4 billion years ago. Cyanobacteria split water for photosynthesis and let the oxygen go as waste, and even by the end of the Great Oxidation Event it had only reached about a tenth of today's level.

Air throws short wavelengths sideways far harder than long ones — the scattering coefficient goes as one over the fourth power of the wavelength. Blue ends up spread across the whole dome; red mostly carries straight on through.
The scattering is done by the air's own molecules — the diatomic gases N2 and O2 — not by dust and not by water vapour. Nitrogen alone is 78.08% of the air.
Warm air is less dense than the air around it, so it rises and cooler air slides in underneath. Wind is that pressure difference levelling itself out.

Sea water has a greater heat capacity than land, so on a sunny day the shore warms and the water barely does. The air over the land rises, and the breeze that comes in off the sea is stronger the wider that temperature gap gets.
Ground finer than sand and coarser than clay, quartz stops being sand and becomes silt. That is mostly how silt gets made in the first place — grain hitting grain while wind, water or ice moves them.
Wind lifts loose dry material straight off the surface — deflation. Roughly half to two thirds of what it takes goes by saltation: grains bouncing along and knocking others loose as they land.

Water vapour will not become a droplet on its own; it needs a surface to land on. Cloud condensation nuclei are about 0.2 micrometres across — a hundredth the size of the droplet that grows on them — and dust, clay, soot and sea salt all serve.

Air that rises expands, and expanding cools it without any heat being taken away. Lift a parcel of damp air far enough and it reaches its dew point, and the vapour it was carrying invisibly turns into drops.
Warm damp air meeting sudden cold condenses in mid-air rather than on a surface, and the droplets are small enough to hang there. Breath on a winter morning is the same thing at arm's length.

Fog and mist are the same droplets. The only thing separating them is visibility: under a kilometre it is fog, and once the sun has evaporated enough of the droplets away for sight to carry further, the same cloud is called mist.
Fog is not its own kind of weather. It is a low stratus cloud that has come down to the ground, and it loses its Latin name the moment it touches.
Cold air moving over water warmer than itself picks up vapour it immediately cannot hold. The fog looks like it is rising off the surface, which is why sailors call it sea smoke.
Cool air past the point where it can hold its vapour and the surplus comes out as liquid on whatever is nearest. That temperature has a name: the dew point.

Grass, leaves and car roofs are not warmed from below by the ground, so on a still night they radiate their heat away and drop past the dew point first. A windy night brings warmer air down onto them and there is no dew at all.
Frost is not frozen dew. Water vapour goes straight from gas to ice on a surface that is below freezing, skipping the liquid stage entirely.
On a clear, still night the ground loses heat to space faster than anything replaces it, so grass and leaves cool below the frost point of the air touching them — colder than the air itself.
Droplets in a cloud are far too light to fall. Turbulence throws them into each other, they fuse into bigger ones, and once a drop is heavy enough to beat air resistance it comes down.
Much of the rain that lands on you arrived as snow. Ice crystals in a freezing cloud grow heavy enough to fall, then melt on the way down through warmer air.

Ice nuclei are far rarer than the nuclei droplets form on, so a cloud can sit well below freezing and still be liquid. Where a crystal does start, water molecules diffuse through the air and freeze onto its surface.

In a cloud holding both ice crystals and supercooled droplets, the ice wins. Crystals grow at the expense of the droplets around them until they are millimetres across and heavy — the Wegener–Bergeron–Findeisen process.

A thunderstorm wants three things: moisture, an unstable air mass, and something to lift it. Sun on the ground supplies the lift, as thermals that keep rising because they stay less dense than what surrounds them.

Wind that changes with height — vertical shear — is what lets a storm organise and go on for hours instead of minutes. The strongest kind it produces, the supercell, is the one that brings large hail and tornadoes.

Charge separates where the updraught is fastest and the cloud is between −15 and −25 °C. Rising ice crystals collide with graupel; the crystals come away positive and the graupel negative, and the cloud ends up sorted top from bottom.
A thundercloud is not the only place charge separates. Lightning also happens in dust storms, forest fires, tornadoes and volcanic eruptions.
The channel reaches about 30,000 K in the 50 microseconds it exists. Air that hot expands faster than sound can get out of its way, and the pulse that leaves is a shock wave.
Light arrives at once and sound does not. Sound covers about 343 metres a second in dry air, so roughly three seconds pass for every kilometre between you and the flash.
A hailstone keeps climbing until the updraught can no longer carry its weight, and in a hail-producing storm that can take half an hour of going up and down.

Hail needs a storm with a good part of its cloud below 0 °C. Droplets carried up there become supercooled and freeze on contact, laying down layers of clear and cloudy ice at least a millimetre thick.

Light refracts going into a raindrop, reflects off the back, and refracts again coming out, and each colour bends by a slightly different amount. Most of it returns at 42°, which is why a rainbow is always the same size and always opposite the sun.
A loose oxygen atom joins an O2 molecule to make O3, with a third body carrying off the spare energy. High in the atmosphere it is ultraviolet below 240 nm that splits O2 to supply those loose atoms.
Ozone is named for its smell — ozein, Greek for 'to smell'. Schönbein got that sharp odour out of sparking electricity through air and recognised it as the one that follows a bolt of lightning.
A tropical cyclone runs on warm water. The thunderstorms that build one need sea surface temperatures around 27 °C, and the cyclone starts to die once it moves over water much below 26.5 °C.

The energy does not come from the wind. It comes from evaporation of water off the ocean surface, which condenses into cloud and rain higher up — the wind is what that release drives, not what drives it.
In a ground blizzard nothing is falling at all. The snow is already on the ground and the wind is picking it up and carrying it, and that alone is enough to take visibility down to 400 m.
A blizzard is defined by wind, not by how much snow falls: sustained winds or gusts of 56 km/h or more, blowing snow cutting visibility to 400 m or less, and three hours or more of it.
A river floods when its flow exceeds what the channel can carry — usually at a bend. Once the surface soil is saturated, infiltration effectively stops and everything that lands afterwards runs off.

Storm surge is the coast flooding because the storm pushed the sea into it: high wind driving water shoreward over a long fetch, and low pressure lifting the sea surface underneath it at the same time.

Sand hitting sand tends to stick where sand hitting hard ground bounces away, so a patch of sand grows itself. Grains bounce up the windward slope, pile at the brink, and avalanche down the far side once the angle of repose is passed — which is how a dune walks downwind.
Loess is nothing but wind-blown dust that landed and stayed. It is mostly silt, and what it weathers into is some of the most agriculturally productive ground on Earth.

Silt-sized grains stay fully suspended rather than bouncing, so wind carries them right out of the desert or the glacial floodplain and drops them far downwind as a blanket. In north-western China that blanket runs over a hundred metres deep.

Lightning going into the ground vaporises and melts the silica it passes through, and what cools behind it is a hollow glass tube following the path the current took. Peak temperature in the channel exceeds 30,000 K.
It does not need sand. A strike on bare rock leaves a glassy crust, or tunnels running through the rock, or in places rock turned wholly to glass.

Steel is iron with carbon in it — between 0.02% and 2.14% by weight. The carbon atoms sit in the iron lattice and stop the planes of iron sliding past each other, which is the whole of why steel is stronger than iron.

Cementation: pack iron bars in charcoal, seal the pot airtight, and heat it from below for a week. Carbon walks into the solid iron without ever melting it. The bars come out about 1% heavier, and they are steel.

About an eighth part tin in copper. Bronze melts near 950 °C, which is cooler than iron will even think about, and it pours into a mould and holds the shape — copper on its own is soft and casts badly.
Arsenic came before tin. Arsenical bronze work-hardens further than pure copper does, so it holds up as something to cut or chop with — and the smiths who made it were breathing arsenic to get there.
Copper and zinc, usually about two to one. The ratio is a dial, not a recipe: move it and the colour, the hardness and how it rings all move with it. That is why there is no single brass.

Sixty-three parts tin to thirty-seven lead melts at 183 °C — below tin's 232 °C and far below lead's 327 °C. A eutectic mixture melts lower than either metal alone, and goes straight from solid to liquid with no mush.
The skin comes off in one piece, and left alone it is not leather yet. Dry it and it goes hard and translucent like a board; wet it again and it starts to rot.
Deerskin was the hide people had long before anyone kept cattle. Untanned it behaves the same way any hide does: board-hard when dry, and rotting as soon as it is wet.
Tannins are polyphenols that bind to proteins and drop them out of solution. Galls are dense with them — the word tannin comes from tan, crushed oak bark, which is where people got them before galls.
Tannins are water-soluble, so steeping the galls pulls them straight out. It is the same extract that makes iron gall ink — the game already turns galls and iron into writing on that basis.

Tannins bind to the collagen in the hide and coat it, so it stops dissolving in water and bacteria can no longer get at it. Raw hide dries hard and rots when wet; tanned hide dries flexible and does not.
Smoke tanning works because smoke carries formaldehyde, and formaldehyde soaks into the hide's cells and gives it some resistance to microbes and to water. Same job as tannin, different molecule.

Tapping: slice a groove into the bark about 6 mm deep with a hooked knife and peel it back. The spiral runs the latex down into a cup. It is a milky colloid — the rubber is suspended in it, not dissolved.

Drive the water off and the suspended particles are forced together into a solid. What is left is cis-1,4-polyisoprene, a single molecule between 100,000 and 1,000,000 daltons — one long chain, over and over.
Latex stays liquid only while it is kept alkaline; add an acid and the particles clump into a solid mass. Ammonia is what plantations add to stop this happening on the way to the factory.

Goodyear dropped a rubber-and-sulfur mix into a hot pan in 1839. Chains of sulfur atoms replace some of the carbon-hydrogen bonds and stitch one polymer chain to the next, and the result stops going soft in the heat.
Canvas is the same over-under plain weave as any cloth, in far heavier yarn — that is the entire difference between a shirt and a sail. Denim is heavy too, but it is twill, not plain weave.

The domestic silk moth eats white mulberry leaves and little else. Thousands of years of breeding have left it unable to fly and unable to live outside human care — it does not exist in the wild at all.
Two or three days of spinning and it has walled itself in behind roughly a mile of filament. Not many short threads wound up — one thread, 300 to 900 metres of it, unbroken.

Boiling water dissolves the sericin gumming the cocoon together and frees the end of the filament, so the whole thing reels off in one continuous length. It also kills the pupa inside, which is the point of doing it now.

The first coins were electrum, a gold-silver alloy that comes out of the ground already mixed. Because the mix varies, nobody could tell what one was worth by looking — which is exactly why a stamp on it was worth something.

A smith works an iron pin down to a taper and heads it, one nail at a time. Until about 1800 that was the only way there was, and nails were valuable enough that people burned abandoned houses down to get them back.

Steel holds an edge because the carbon lets it be hardened: cool it fast from red heat and the carbon is trapped in the lattice as martensite. That comes out harder than you want and brittle, so it is then tempered back.

Blades ran stone, then copper, then bronze, then iron, then steel. A bronze blade cannot be hardened by quenching the way steel can — it is hammered hard instead, and it is cast to shape rather than forged.
A point is easy. The eye is not: you are drilling a hole through a sliver of bone without splitting it, and that was the limit on how fine a needle could get. Ones like this are 50,000 years old.

Twist fibres into a yarn one way, twist yarns into a strand the other way, twist strands into a rope the first way again. Nothing is tied or glued: it is the successive counter-twists fighting each other that hold a rope together.

The potter's wheel came first — one in western Ukraine dates to the middle of the 5th millennium BC, before anything rolled a cart. The wheels that followed were plain wooden disks with a hole cut for the axle.

A candle carries its fuel as a solid it has to melt first. A lamp keeps a pool of it liquid and lets the wick reach down — so it burns as long as the bowl holds out, and can be refilled without going out.

Hollow a stone, fill it with animal fat, lay a wick in it. The oldest one found is from Lascaux, in a cave people lived in 10,000 to 15,000 years ago — light that far underground had to be carried in.
The oldest leather shoe known is 5,500 years old, from a cave at Areni in Armenia. One piece of hide, gathered up around the foot — and the laces survived with it.
Cut from a single piece and pulled closed with a lace, no sole and no seams to speak of. That is what the Areni-1 shoe is, and it is the oldest leather footwear anyone has found.

Plumbing is named after the metal: plumbum. Lead was the pipe material for centuries because it is soft enough to beat and bend into shape cold — the same softness that lets it leave the pipe and end up in the water.

A scratch plough only opens a furrow. A share cuts the sod horizontally under the surface and the mouldboard lifts and turns it over — which is what finally made the heavy soils of northern Europe workable.
Dead plants normally rot away entirely. Under mud or in sour water the oxygen never reaches them, decay stalls part-done, and the carbon stays where it fell. That backlog is peat.
Mud over the top is what does it: it keeps oxygen off the dead plant matter, so it cannot finish rotting. Acidic water does the same job by a different route.
Bury a peat bog under sediment and leave it for millions of years. Heat and pressure drive out the water, the methane and the carbon dioxide, and what stays behind is progressively more carbon.

Heat coal with the air shut out and it does not burn — it comes apart. The point of doing it is the coke that stays behind, for iron and steel; the black tar that runs off is the by-product that built organic chemistry.
Phenol is an alcohol that is acidic, which almost no alcohol is. Lye neutralises it into sodium phenolate; the neutral oils in the tar do nothing. Runge got the first phenol out of coal tar in 1834.
The same trick as charcoal, but keeping what boils off instead of what stays. Heat wood with no air and tar and pitch drip out of it — and among the vapours are methanol and acetic acid.
Wood alcohol, and it is called that because this is where it came from. It boils at 64.7 °C, so it comes over first and well ahead of the water. Four millilitres of it can destroy the optic nerve.
Two methanol and one oxygen give two formaldehyde and two water. It is the single biggest thing methanol is used for, and most of that formaldehyde goes on to become a polymer.

The oxidation will not go usefully on its own; it needs a catalyst, and the usual one is plain silver metal. The silver is not consumed — it only makes the reaction take a path it would not otherwise take.

Curd is casein, and casein is a protein — so formaldehyde cross-links it exactly as it cross-links any other. The result is a hard plastic made out of milk, and it was in buttons, pens and piano keys from 1897.

Phenol and formaldehyde condense into a three-dimensional network rather than long separate chains, which is why the result is infusible: there is nothing left to slide. Baekeland, 1907, and the first plastic with no natural part in it.

Ethanol boils at 78.2 °C and water at 100, so heat drives the alcohol off first. Distilling stops at 95.6% though: past that the two boil together as one mixture and no amount of redistilling will separate them.

Yeast eats the sugar and gives back ethanol and carbon dioxide. Brazil runs this at industrial scale not for drinking but for feedstock — cane ethanol is the front end of a route to plastic that never touches oil.

Take the water out of ethanol and what is left is ethylene. Hot vapour over alumina will do it, or sulfuric acid will. More ethylene is made each year than any other organic compound — over 225 million tonnes.

Fawcett and Gibson put ethylene under several hundred atmospheres at ICI in 1933 and found a white waxy solid. The molecules had joined end to end into chains. It is now the most used plastic in the world.

ICI could not repeat their own discovery at first. The reaction had been started by a trace of oxygen leaking into the apparatus — the contamination was the initiator, and without knowing that they had no experiment.
Rock has no single melting point. Wet granite starts to go near 650 °C; wet basalt holds out to about 1,080 °C at surface pressure. Past that, any stone is magma.
Above about 650 °C rock melts in patches rather than all at once. The melt gathers in pale streaks through the solid remains — migmatite, and the rock cycle closing on itself.
Magma is the melt while it is still underground. The moment it is expelled onto the surface and meets the air, nothing about the liquid changes except the word for it: it is lava now.
Magma stuck underground cools over thousands of years, and crystals have time to grow. That is the whole difference: granite's quartz, feldspar and mica are big enough to pick out by eye.
At the surface the same melt loses its heat in days. Crystals start everywhere at once and none of them get large, so basalt is dark, dense and too fine-grained to see the grains in.
Lava running into the sea is quenched on contact. The skin freezes, the flow swells behind it and bursts out as the next lobe: pillow basalt, and it is what the ocean floor is made of.
Silica-rich lava is stiff, and stiffness stops atoms moving far enough to line up. Nucleation never starts, so it sets as glass — one continuous solid with no crystal anywhere in it.
Lava carries water and carbon dioxide dissolved in it under pressure. Erupted, the pressure drops, the gas comes out of solution all at once, and the froth freezes before it can escape.
Granite is not a substance but a mixture, grown into itself: quartz, alkali feldspar, mica and plagioclase. The feldspar is the pale blocky part, the quartz the grey glassy grains between.
Silicon dioxide. Every silicon sits in a cage of four oxygens and every oxygen is shared with the next cage — a framework with no weak plane in it, which is why quartz is so hard to wear out.
Water heated by a body of magma dissolves silica, carries it up through cracks and drops it again as it cools. A quartz vein is a crack that hot water filled from the inside.
Feldspars are aluminium tectosilicates: a silica framework with aluminium substituted into it and sodium, potassium or calcium tucked in to balance the charge. Sixty per cent of the crust.
Rain is faintly acidic and it hydrolyses feldspar: the sodium and potassium wash out, and what stays is clay — illite, smectite, kaolinite. Nearly all the clay in the world was feldspar first.
Acid in rain and soil water hydrolyses granite's feldspar into clay, which washes away. Quartz has the lowest weathering potential of any of it and does not go, so quartz grains are what is left.
Basalt weathers faster than granite: finer grain, glass between the crystals, and iron that rusts. Breaking down it releases calcium, sodium and magnesium, and leaves clay and iron oxides behind.
Bury mud under more mud and the weight presses the water out of the pore space until the grains lock together. Mudrocks are half of all the sedimentary rock in the record.
Press it harder and the flat clay flakes all rotate to lie the same way. That alignment is fissility: shale is mudstone that has learned to split into sheets.
Sand buried under more sand compacts, and the warmth at depth makes minerals crystallise in the gaps and glue the grains to each other. That cement is the difference between sand and a rock.
A dune buried by the next dune keeps its shape. Its steep slip faces survive as cross-bedding in sets metres thick, and you can still read the old wind direction straight off the cliff.
Water only carries stones that size at high flow. By the time a flood drops them they are rounded from the journey, and finer sediment settles into the gaps and cements the lot together.

Metamorphism begins around 150–200 °C. The clay recrystallises, and the new grains grow across the direction of the squeeze rather than along the bedding — so slate splits at an angle to its own layers.
By about 400 °C the mica has grown from microscopic to merely small. Still too fine to pick out one flake, but together they give the cleavage surface a silky, sometimes golden sheen.
Past 500 °C the mica flakes grow big enough to see with a hand lens, all oriented the same way. The rock now splits into plates you can hold rather than sheets you can bend.
Over 600 °C the minerals stop mixing and start sorting: pale quartz and feldspar into one band, dark mica and amphibole into the next. The striping is what makes it gneiss and not schist.
Heat and tectonic pressure recrystallise the quartz grains into one another until cement and grain are the same thing. Break quartzite and the fracture goes through the grains, not around them.
A body of magma bakes the rock it pushes into. In limestone the small calcite crystals dissolve and regrow larger and interlocked, and the bedding and fossils are modified or destroyed with them.
Buried under later sediment, peat compresses and gives up water. Lignite forms below 100 °C, mostly by microbes rather than by heat, and can still be three-quarters water when it is dug.

Buried deep enough to reach 85 °C, coal keeps maturing: water and oxygen leave, carbon concentrates to about 84%, and it hardens and blackens into bituminous coal. Temperature matters more than pressure.
Above about 235 °C the bitumen in bituminous coal breaks down and leaves. What stays is 86–97% carbon, hard, glossy and almost smokeless: the highest rank coal reaches.
Carbon only takes the diamond arrangement under real pressure: about 4.5 gigapascals at 950 °C, which means 150 km down. Every diamond at the surface was carried up by a volcano.
Aluminium oxide, packed tight enough to score 9 on the Mohs scale — only diamond is harder. Pure corundum is transparent and colourless; everything interesting about it is an impurity.
Swap a little of the aluminium for chromium and the crystal starts absorbing green and violet light. What gets through is red. That is the entire difference between ruby and colourless corundum.

Blue needs two impurities, not one. Where an iron and a titanium ion sit side by side in place of aluminium, an electron hops between them; the energy it takes is yellow light, and blue is what is left.
Emerald is beryl — a beryllium aluminium silicate — with traces of chromium, or sometimes vanadium. The same chromium that makes ruby red makes emerald green: the host crystal decides the colour.
Silica dissolved in water is put down again in cracks, not as crystal but as microscopic spheres with water still trapped between them. Sized evenly enough, they diffract light into colours.
Schist is mostly mica already, all lying the same way. Crushed, it lets the flakes go whole rather than shattering them — which is where most of the world's flake mica actually comes from.
Granite's third mineral, and the one that gives. Its sheets are held to each other by weak bonds, so it comes away in elastic plates; single books of it in coarse granite can be feet across.

Light does not come in a smooth stream. Cut it finer and finer and you reach a piece that cannot be divided: one quantum of the electromagnetic field, massless, and moving at one fixed speed and no other.

Heat free electrons and they radiate. Each time one swerves past a nucleus it loses kinetic energy, and that energy leaves as a photon. The German name means braking radiation, and it is what an X-ray tube emits.

The Sun is not a burning ball of gas. At that temperature hydrogen's electrons are stripped off their nuclei, and what is left conducts electricity and answers to magnetic fields. An estimated 99.9% of ordinary matter is in this state.

It takes 13.6 electronvolts — an ultraviolet photon at 91.2 nanometres — to knock the electron off a hydrogen atom. Hot young stars pour those out, and the cloud around them ends up ionised. That is an H II region.

Above about 1.66 trillion kelvin, protons and neutrons stop holding together. Quarks and gluons come unconfined and move freely — the state the whole universe was in for its first twenty microseconds.
Beta decay seen from the inside. A down quark of charge −1/3 emits a W boson and becomes an up quark of charge +2/3. Do that to one quark in a neutron and the neutron is now a proton.

A proton is three quarks: two up and one down, bound so hard by the strong force that nobody has ever pulled one out to look at it. The charge is just the fractions adding up — 2/3 plus 2/3 minus 1/3 is exactly 1.
Swap one quark and you swap the particle. Two downs and an up is a neutron: −1/3 minus 1/3 plus 2/3 is zero. Being uncharged is why it can walk straight into a nucleus that would push a proton away.

A neutron inside a nucleus can last forever. A free one has a mean life of about fifteen minutes and then decays into a proton, an electron and an antineutrino. Nothing does it to the neutron; it simply runs out.

For its first 378,000 years the universe was too hot for this — every electron was knocked loose again. When it finally cooled enough for electrons and protons to stay bound, light stopped scattering and got out. We still see that light.

The strong force binds protons and neutrons over about a femtometre and no further. What it makes is tens of thousands of times smaller than the atom around it and holds very nearly all of that atom's mass.

Take the two electrons off a helium atom and what is left is two protons and two neutrons — an alpha particle. It is the same object that comes out of decaying uranium: a nucleus with nothing around it.

A nucleus has energy levels the way an atom does, only about a million times further apart. Excite one and it drops back almost immediately, and the photon it lets go is a gamma ray: light, at nuclear energies.

Above 1.022 MeV — exactly twice an electron's rest mass — a gamma ray passing close to a nucleus can vanish and leave an electron and a positron behind. The nucleus has to be there to take the recoil.
Ionisation is the cut: electron on one side, ion on the other, both free to move independently. That is why a plasma conducts, and why the electrons in one can be treated as a gas in their own right.

A neutron that wanders into ordinary hydrogen is simply kept, and the 2.223 MeV it no longer needs leaves as a gamma ray. That exact line is seen coming off solar flares. What remains is hydrogen with a neutron in it.

Do it again. A deuterium nucleus catches a second neutron and becomes tritium — one proton, two neutrons. It is how heavy-water reactors end up with tritium in them whether anybody wanted it there or not.
The usual route. Lithium-6 in a neutron flux splits into helium and tritium. Tritium's half-life is 12.32 years, so there is no natural stock of it anywhere to dig up — all of it has to be made.

The easiest fusion there is, because both nuclei carry only a single positive charge to push each other apart. They make an unstable helium-5 that instantly throws off a neutron carrying 14.1 MeV; the helium keeps 3.5. Total, 17.6 MeV.

A uranium-235 nucleus that absorbs a neutron becomes uranium-236 for an instant, then splits into two lighter nuclei and a couple of spare neutrons. About 200 MeV per event, and both halves come out radioactive.

Fission fragments come out with more neutrons than a stable nucleus of their mass can carry. They beta-decay their way back down, and the nuclei left behind shed what is still spare as gamma rays. That goes on for centuries.

At the Sun's core temperature of 15.5 million kelvin, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium by the proton–proton chain. It is the dominant process in stars the size of the Sun and smaller. It is where sunlight comes from.

Six times hotter than the Sun's core, alpha particles fuse fast enough to get past the beryllium-8 barrier — beryllium-8 lasts 8×10⁻¹⁷ of a second — and three of them become carbon-12. Every carbon atom in this game was made this way.

Carbon-12 catches one more helium nucleus and becomes oxygen-16, letting 7.16 MeV go as a gamma ray. Carbon, then oxygen, one alpha particle at a time — the two elements every living thing is built from, made in the same place.

Above 500 million kelvin, in stars of at least four solar masses, carbon starts fusing with carbon. Out of it comes a mixture mainly of oxygen, neon, sodium and magnesium — the next rung of a ladder that ends at iron.

The explosion makes radioactive nickel-56, which decays to cobalt-56 with a 6-day half-life and then to iron-56 with a 77.3-day one. That decay is what keeps a supernova glowing for months, and the iron it leaves is thrown out across the galaxy.

Two neutron stars merge, and in the neutron-rich wreckage nuclei catch neutrons faster than they can decay. That is the r-process, and in 2017 it was finally caught happening. Models put 3 to 13 Earth masses of gold in a single merger.

In about five billion years the Sun will run out of hydrogen in its core, start burning it in a shell around the core instead, and swell. It takes Mercury and Venus with it, and most likely the Earth.

Nothing starts a star but its own weight. A dense region of a molecular cloud collapses, heats as it compresses, and stops falling only when the pressure inside can hold it up. Fusion begins after that, not before.

Core hydrogen runs out, fusion moves to a shell around the dead core, and the outer layers swell to tens or hundreds of times the Sun's radius and cool to red as they go. Every star that lives long enough does this.

An ageing giant can lose 50 to 70% of its whole mass to its own stellar wind. The gas drifts off at a few kilometres a second, ultraviolet from the exposed core lights it up, and the display lasts about 10,000 years.

What the wind leaves. No fusion and no heat holding it up — only electron degeneracy pressure, which is not a force but a rule about how electrons may be stacked. The Sun's mass in an Earth-sized volume: a tonne per cubic centimetre.

Dust is made in the cooling outflow of dying stars. Silicates come off the oxygen-rich ones, graphite and amorphous carbon off the carbon-rich ones, and the stellar wind carries the grains out into the galaxy.

A molecular cloud is mostly hydrogen in molecular form, with carbon monoxide a distant second, and enough dust mixed through it to shield the inside from the ultraviolet that would otherwise pull the molecules apart.

A massive star builds shells of heavier and heavier ash until the core is iron — and iron gives nothing back, because fusing it costs energy instead of releasing it. With nothing holding it up any more, the core falls in and the star comes apart.

The other kind. A white dwarf pulling gas off a companion creeps up on the Chandrasekhar limit — about 1.44 solar masses — and detonates. They all go off at nearly the same brightness, which is how the expansion of the universe got measured.

The core falls and does not stop until it reaches the density of a nucleus. On the way down, electrons and protons are pressed together into neutrons and a flood of neutrinos leaves. 1.4 solar masses in a ball ten kilometres across.

Dust also condenses inside the expanding wreckage as it cools. A supernova is one of the places the grains come from, alongside red giants, carbon stars and novae — and it seeds a far wider volume than a stellar wind ever reaches.

Neutrons resist being packed, but only so far. The smallest black holes made this way are thought to start somewhere between two and four solar masses. Past that nothing known holds the core up, and it falls to a surface light cannot cross back out of.

Grains stick, clumps grow, and somewhere near a kilometre across the body's own gravity takes over from whatever was making them stick. After that it pulls in the rest. How anything gets past a metre wide is still an open problem.

Planetesimals collide and combine into Moon-sized embryos over roughly 0.1 to 1 million years. Then the embryos collide with each other, and that part takes 10 to 100 million more. A planet is the last one left in its orbit.

The ones that never finished. Jupiter's orbital resonances threw out more than 99% of the planetesimals in the belt, so what was left could never assemble into anything. The whole belt now weighs 3% of the Moon.

Rock and dust mixed with frozen water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, methane and ammonia. Bring one near the Sun and those ices go straight to gas, which is the coma; the solar wind pushes it out into a tail.

A solid core of about ten Earth masses is the threshold. Past it the core starts pulling hydrogen and helium straight off the disc, and the remaining 90% of the planet's mass arrives in roughly ten thousand years.

Astronomers call water, ammonia and methane 'ices', and that is mostly what these are. Only about 20% of an ice giant is hydrogen and helium, against more than 90% for Jupiter and Saturn. Uranus and Neptune are the two we have.

About 4.4 billion years ago a Mars-sized body called Theia hit the proto-Earth. Roughly a fifth of Theia ended up as a ring of debris around the Earth, and about half of that ring re-accreted into the Moon.
A bacterium's DNA is not shut in a nucleus. It sits loose in the cytoplasm as one circular chromosome, with the ribosomes right there beside it.
The membrane is the tell. Archaea join their lipids with ether bonds where every bacterium and every animal uses ester bonds, and some live in pools saltier than anything else can stand.
One cell swallowed another and did not digest it. Every plant, animal and fungus alive descends from that merger, and carries the swallowed thing still.
Break a cell open and this is the evidence: a single circular DNA molecule like a bacterium's, and ribosomes closer to a bacterium's than to the cell's own.
The organelle kept its old job. Aerobic respiration happens inside it, not in the cell around it, and it hands out the ATP the whole cell spends.
Around two billion years ago a free-living cyanobacterium got inside a cell and stayed. It is generally held to have happened once, and every green thing descends from it.
An alga is a cell that acquired photosynthesis rather than inventing it. No roots, no stems, no leaves — and the machinery inside is borrowed.
Photosynthesis has an address. Carbon dioxide is fixed into sugar inside the chloroplast, in the Calvin cycle, and nowhere else in the plant.

Lactobacillus bulgaricus and Streptococcus thermophilus ferment the sugars in milk and produce lactic acid, and that acid acting on the milk protein is what gives yoghurt its texture and its tartness.
In shallow water they grow as mats over the sediment, and the mats trap grains and build upward. The structures they leave are among the oldest clear signs of life on Earth.
They need almost nothing: light, air, and enough water to switch on. Bare rock that is briefly damp is a habitat, and they are usually the first thing in it.
They invented oxygenic photosynthesis and then ran it for a billion years. The air we breathe is one organism's accumulated waste product.
Algae are not confined to open water. Given light and enough moisture to stay active they will grow on soil, on rock, and in the film on any wet surface.
The mould on damp timber is a fungus already — the visible fuzz is its mycelium. Fungi are the principal decomposers of plant material.
The mushroom is not the fungus. It is a fruiting body the mycelium puts up when conditions suit, and almost all of the organism stays underground.
Wind is how most fungi travel. The spores are single cells built to be light, and moving air is the whole dispersal strategy.
That is what a mushroom is for. The fruiting body exists to make spores and drop them, and some species fire them off explosively.
A spore lands and puts out one thread, which branches, and branches again. That tangle in the soil is the fungus; everything else it does is a side effect.
Give a fungus dead plant stalks and it will run through them. Decomposing plant material is what mycelium is for, and straw is nothing but that.
Two kingdoms in one body. The fungus builds the structure and holds the water; the alga inside makes the food. Neither one is a lichen on its own.
The photosynthetic partner can be a cyanobacterium instead. And where that partner can live perfectly well on its own, the arrangement looks less like a partnership than like parasitism.
They pull mineral grains out of bare rock with their filaments and then dissolve them. Weathering under lichen cover ran three to four times faster than on newly exposed rock.
Root and fungus grow into one organ. The fungal threads reach past the strip of soil the root has already stripped of phosphate, and the plant pays for the reach in sugar.
On trees the fungus sheathes the root tip without ever entering a cell — a different arrangement from the one in most herbs, where the threads push through the cell wall.
Phosphate barely moves in soil, so a root empties the ground it touches and then starves beside plenty. The fungus is not a bonus; for most plants it is the supply line.
The plant builds the bacteria a house. A root hair curls around them, an infection thread carries them inward, and the root swells into an organ that exists only for them.
Soybeans, clover, alfalfa, peanuts, lupins — the whole legume family does this. It is the reason a legume can be grown on ground too poor for a cereal.
Cut one open and it is red inside. That is leghaemoglobin, near-identical to the myoglobin in meat, and the plant makes it to keep oxygen away from the bacteria's enzyme.
Four fifths of the air is nitrogen almost nothing can touch. Nitrogenase breaks the triple bond anyway, at a cost of sixteen ATP for one molecule, and hands over ammonia.
This is the doorway. Fixed nitrogen is stuck onto a carbon skeleton as glutamate, and every amino acid downstream gets its nitrogen from there.
A body plan with almost nothing in it: two layers of cells around a sac, and one hole that serves as mouth and as exit.
Free-swimming single-celled algae, drifting in the water until something takes them in. They are dinoflagellates, mostly of one genus, and they live perfectly well without a host.
The algae move into vacuoles inside the animal's own cells and hand over sugar. Up to 90% of what a coral lives on is made by something that is not the coral.
The polyp lays down aragonite underneath itself and sits in the cup it built. The white branching thing sold in a shop is not the animal — it is the animal's floor.
A reef is generations of skeleton with a living skin on top. Under 0.1% of the ocean's area, and at least a quarter of all marine species live on it.
Vertically, a healthy tropical reef gains somewhere between one and twenty-five centimetres a year. The living structure on top of most reefs is six to eight thousand years old.
Darwin's explanation, and it was right: the volcanic island the reef grew around sinks, the coral keeps building upward to stay in the light, and a ring is left with a lagoon inside.
About a degree above the usual monthly maximum, held for weeks, and the animal throws its algae out. What goes white is the bare skeleton showing through tissue that has lost its colour.
Most leaf litter is torn to pieces by soil animals before any microbe finishes it. Breaking it small is the point: it multiplies the surface the decomposers can work on.
Some worms keep a permanent vertical burrow and drag whole leaves down into it. Lumbricus terrestris does this; the word for it is anecic.
They are not escaping drowning — they breathe through their skin and can survive days underwater. A wet surface just lets them travel further above ground than they ever could below it.
What is left when the decomposers have taken everything easy. Most of the humus in most soils has been sitting there more than a hundred years without being touched.
A heap needs about twenty-five parts carbon to one of nitrogen: dry brown stalks and wet green waste in the right proportion. Get it right and the pile heats itself to 54–71 °C.
The other method, and it never gets hot. Worms eat the material and what comes out the other end is the product — castings, five times richer in available nitrogen than the soil around them.
Finished compost is not the end of it. The easily eaten fraction keeps going and what survives is the stable remainder, which is what actually stays in the soil.
Sand holds nothing. Humus can carry 80–90% of its own weight in water, and it is negatively charged, so it holds nutrient ions too. Adding it is what turns grit into ground.
The plant chains glucose into fibre. One bond is flipped relative to starch — β rather than α — and that single difference is the most abundant organic polymer on Earth.
Grind up a plant and this is most of what is left. Wood is 40–50% cellulose and cotton fibre is 90%; it is the material plants build their cell walls out of.
The biggest of a ruminant's stomach compartments, and there is not one cellulose-digesting enzyme of the cow's own anywhere in it. Everything that works in there belongs to something else.
This is why a cow lives on grass and you cannot. Microbes ferment the fibre into acetate, propionate and butyrate, and those cross the rumen wall straight into the blood.
The cow never gets the grass itself. What reaches its blood is what the microbes excreted, and the milk is built from that. Then it digests the microbes too, for the protein.
Nectar is the fuel and pollen is the food. Bees pack it into baskets on their back legs and carry it home, where it ferments into bee bread and feeds the brood.
A pollen grain is not a sperm cell. It is a whole small organism, a gametophyte, sealed in sporopollenin — a wall tough enough that pollen survives in sediment long after the plant is gone.
Pollination is not fertilisation. The grain lands, grows a tube down through the style, and delivers two sperm: one makes the embryo, the other makes the food packed in beside it.
Magnetite is only weakly magnetic until something magnetises it. The leading explanation is a lightning strike: the field around the bolt is strong enough, and the Earth's own 0.5 gauss is not.

Draw a lodestone along a piece of iron, always the same way, and the iron's magnetic domains turn to face the same direction. Hard iron holds that alignment once the lodestone is gone; annealed iron lets it go.

Wire is not cast, it is pulled — cold, through a die narrower than the metal going in. The volume cannot change, so as the diameter falls the length rises. Copper takes this better than almost any other metal.
Move a magnet near a coil of wire and a current appears in the coil; hold it still and nothing happens. It is the change in the field that does it, which is why a generator has to keep turning.
Ørsted noticed in 1820 that a compass needle near a live wire swings sideways. A current makes a magnetic field looping around the wire, and electricity and magnetism turned out to be one subject.
Scatter iron filings on paper over a magnet and they line up end to end. They are showing the field: the region around the magnet where it can twist another magnet or deflect a moving charge.
A permanent magnet cannot be turned off; this one can. Wind the wire into a coil so each turn's field adds to the next, and the field lasts exactly as long as the current does and no longer.
The iron is not there for strength. A ferromagnetic core concentrates the flux through the coil and can take the field to thousands of times what the same coil would manage on its own.

A magnetic field pushes sideways on a wire carrying current, and that push turns the rotor. Half a turn on the push would reverse, so a commutator swaps the current over each half turn and the torque never changes sign.

Two coils on one iron ring, touching nowhere. A changing current in the first makes a changing flux in the core, which induces a voltage in the second in the ratio of the turns. Hold the current steady and nothing crosses.

Volta stacked pairs of zinc and copper discs in 1800, every pair separated by card soaked in brine. The salt water is not packing: without it there is no path for ions, and a stack of dry discs does nothing at all.

Copper was not the only choice — Volta's pile worked with silver discs too. What matters is that the two metals are different, so they give up electrons at different rates and charge has somewhere to go.
A current is charge in motion, and it needs a loop. Join the top of the pile to the bottom with wire and the free electrons in the copper drift along it — at five amps, about a millimetre a second.
About 80% of the world's electricity is made this way: boil water, let the steam spin a turbine, let the turbine spin a generator. Whatever the fuel, its only job is heating water.
A wind turbine is a generator on a stick. No turbine can take all the wind's energy, because the air has to keep moving to get out of the way; Betz's law caps the share at 16/27, about 59%.
Eighty per cent nickel, twenty per cent chromium. The alloy has around 66 times copper's resistivity, so current has to force its way through, and what it spends forcing comes out as heat.

Heat goes as the current squared times the resistance, so a resistive wire is a heater. Nichrome survives being one: the first time it glows it grows a chromium-oxide skin that oxygen cannot get through.

Make the wire fine enough and resistive heating carries it past 2,500 °C, hot enough to radiate visible light rather than only warmth. Only tungsten will stand there: it melts at 3,422 °C, higher than any other metal.
Before tungsten, the filament was carbon. It glowed well enough to sell, but a filament evaporates while it works and the vapour lands on the inside of the glass, darkening the bulb as it burns.

The filament sits at white heat, where oxygen would eat it in seconds. The glass is there to keep the air out — and it also collects the tungsten that boils off, which is why an old bulb looks smoked.

A vacuum is not the best filling. Argon slows the tungsten boiling off the wire by giving the atoms something to bounce back from, at the price of carrying heat away — the gas cools the filament even as it saves it.

Krypton is heavier than argon and worse at conducting heat, so it steals less warmth from the filament while still holding the tungsten in. It is also far more expensive, which is why most bulbs used argon.
The dioxide from burning sulfur is passed over vanadium oxide with more oxygen to make the trioxide, and that taken up in water is sulfuric acid. Nearly all the world's supply is made this way.

Lead on one side, lead dioxide on the other, sulfuric acid between. Discharging turns both plates to lead sulfate and consumes the acid — and the whole reaction runs backwards if you push current the other way.

Planté grew his plates rather than fitting them: two lead sheets in acid, charged and discharged over and over until the dioxide layer built up. It was the first battery that could be refilled instead of replaced.

Push current through water and it comes apart — hydrogen at one electrode, oxygen at the other, twice as much hydrogen by volume. Pure water barely conducts, so something has to be dissolved in it first.

Salt water conducts about a hundred thousand times better than pure water. The dissolved ions run to the electrodes and cancel the charge piling up there, and that is what lets the current keep flowing.

Make the object the cathode and a bar of copper the anode. The bar dissolves into the bath as ions, the ions come out of solution onto the object, and the bath never runs down — the metal just moves across.
The layer can be thinner than anything you could beat or cast, because it arrives an ion at a time. Silver plate is a base-metal object made the cathode in a bath of dissolved silver.

Boron has three outer electrons where silicon has four, so every boron atom in the lattice leaves one bond unfinished. Those gaps shift when a neighbouring electron drops into one, and the crystal conducts by moving holes.
Phosphorus brings five outer electrons into a lattice with room to share only four. The fifth is barely held, comes loose at room temperature and wanders, so the crystal conducts by moving electrons.

Put the two in one crystal and the loose electrons fall into the nearby holes, leaving a stripped band at the seam with a field across it. Charge crosses that seam easily one way and hardly at all the other.

Drive current the way the junction allows and electrons are pushed across into the holes. Each one that drops in gives up the band gap's worth of energy as a single photon, and the size of the gap sets the colour.
Sandwich a thin slice of p-type between two n-type regions and you have two junctions back to back. A small current into the middle layer then controls a much larger one through the whole stack.

It works inverted too, a thin n-type layer between two p-type regions. Either way the middle layer is thin on purpose, so most of what enters one side carries straight on across instead of leaking out of the base.

A photon knocks an electron up out of its bond and leaves a hole behind. Near the junction the built-in field sweeps the two apart before they can fall back together, and that separation is a voltage.

Air is four-fifths nitrogen that almost nothing alive can use. At 250 to 350 bar over iron at 450 to 550 °C it joins with hydrogen — and about half the nitrogen in your body came through this reaction.

The motor drives a compressor, not a cooler. Squeezed ammonia condenses at the back of the cabinet and gives its heat to the room; let through a valve it boils inside, and boiling takes that heat back out of the food.
Nothing here makes cold. A fluid boils in the coils inside the box and carries heat out with it, and the water has nowhere to put its own heat except into that fluid, so it gives it up and freezes.
Thyroid peroxidase hangs iodine onto particular tyrosine residues inside thyroglobulin, then couples two iodinated rings together. Thyroxine is two tyrosines joined, carrying four iodine atoms.

Plants build ascorbate from glucose along the Smirnoff-Wheeler pathway, by way of L-galactose, which a dehydrogenase oxidises to the lactone. Animals reach the same molecule from the same sugar by a different road ending at L-gulonolactone oxidase.

Prolyl 4-hydroxylase hydroxylates proline after the chain is already built, and it cannot run without ascorbate. Vitamin C's job here is narrow and specific: cycling the enzyme's iron between Fe2+ and Fe3+.

Glycine-X-Y, over and over: the centre of the rope is so tight that only glycine's single hydrogen fits. Hydroxyproline's hydroxyl makes no hydrogen bond at all — it holds proline in its trans form, and that alone stabilises the helix.
Ca10(PO4)6(OH)2 — calcium phosphate with a hydroxide sitting in the lattice. It is 65 to 70% of the mass of bone and 70 to 80% of dentin and enamel. This is the mineral half of every skeleton.

The mineral does not coat the collagen, it grows between the fibres. Collagen carries the tension, the hydroxyapatite crystals interspersed through it carry the compression, and bone runs about 30% matrix to 70% mineral by mass.
Fluoride takes the place of the hydroxide in the apatite lattice. What comes out is stronger and more acid-resistant than the hydroxyapatite it replaced — the same crystal with one ion swapped.

Four pyrrole rings closed into a macrocycle, their four nitrogens pointing inward at a pocket exactly the size of one metal ion. In animals the whole ring is built from glycine condensed with succinyl-CoA out of the citric acid cycle.

Ferrochelatase drops a ferrous iron into the middle of protoporphyrin IX and the ring's four nitrogens clamp it as a tetradentate ligand. That single iron is what binds oxygen, reversibly, in every breath.

Four globular subunits, each holding one heme, so one molecule carries up to four oxygens. The first one bound reshapes the sites for the next — which is why the binding curve is a sigmoid rather than the usual hyperbola.
One globin unit, one heme, no cooperativity, and a higher affinity for oxygen than haemoglobin has — so muscle takes oxygen off blood and keeps it. Whales and seals carry muscle unusually full of it.

The same macrocycle as heme with magnesium in the middle instead of iron, and one ring reduced to make a chlorin. It absorbs hard in the blue and the red and badly in the green — green is the light it does not use.
B12 is built on a corrin ring — porphyrin's close relative — with cobalt at the centre. This is the only place biology uses cobalt at all, and only archaea and bacteria can make it.

The oxygen-evolving complex is four manganese ions and one calcium in a single cluster, wired to the P680 chlorophyll. It steps through five states, S0 to S4, because splitting water is a four-electron job and light arrives one photon at a time.
2 H2O → O2 + 4 H+ + 4 e-. The manganese cluster is what makes that arithmetic possible: it banks oxidising equivalents one at a time until it has four, then lets the oxygen go.
Cysteine desulfurase strips the sulfur off a cysteine, leaving alanine behind, and that sulfide is what the cluster is built from. Four more cysteines then hold the finished cube onto the protein.
